segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Well, good evening, everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: My name's Gary Payne, and I'll be the leader for your walking holiday in Spain.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And the purpose of this evening's meeting is for us all to get to know each other in advance and for you to ask any questions you may have about the holiday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So I'll begin by telling you a little bit about what to expect now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The ferry crossing from England to Santander in Spain takes about 24 hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We'll be sailing on the Prince Regent, which was first launched in the 1980s, as well as the crew of 160.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It can accommodate about 2000 people and 600 cars and its sales at an average speed of 37 kilometers an hour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: There'll be an on board map on one of the decks which charts the ship's progress during the voyage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Although our mini bus will be on one of the vehicle decks in the boat, access to these decks is prohibited during the crossing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So when you leave our bus, you'll have to take everything that you're likely to need with you, like toiletries or books and magazines.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: In fact, it's probably a good idea to put these things in a separate bag beforehand.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: You shouldn't need snacks on board as meals are provided, and they're quite substantial.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And if you don't feel well or get a headache, you can get tablets from me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I always carry an adequate supply.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Now, once we're in Spain, we'll be based at a hostel in a small village called La Vega de la Barna, about 120 kilometers from Santander.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It's a very picturesque area that's retained a lot of its traditional industry and culture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The hostel accommodations are fairly simple.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: There are bunk beds and each room holds 4 to 8 people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: But the bathrooms and showers are of a high standard.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The hostel residents have the use of tennis courts nearby.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: If you feel like a game, we'll be given breakfast and an evening meal at the hostel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: In general, the hostel is relaxed, but there are a few rules which the owners enforce strictly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Smoking is not allowed anywhere inside the building and food and drink is banned in the dormitories.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Any chairs or tables which you take outside into the gardens must be returned every evening to their original place.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And finally, the doors are locked after midnight, out of consideration for other guests who are trying to sleep.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It's a very popular area for tourists because of its spectacular peaks, although they're only 25 kilometers from the sea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The highest peaks are more than 2600 meters high and have year round snow caps on the highest peaks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Good morning and welcome back to the series of linguistics lectures.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Today I will be talking about the language Bish Llama, which is a form of pidgin English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Linguists use the term pidgin to describe new languages that are created by combining two or more existing languages, often in a simplified form.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The study of pidgin languages is important because it provides us with information about language change and modification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The Pidgin English known as Bish Llama, is used in the South Pacific nation of Vanuatu, a group of islands where 81/1 languages are still regularly used by the local people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: There are a further 17 local languages that are in danger of dying out and eight that have been identified as extinct.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: This gives a total of 106/1 languages in all, a very high number for a small country with a population of just 200,000 people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Then thinking about foreign languages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: English is the most important and has official status, largely because it is the medium for all education purposes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: However, it has been lamented as the most widely spoken language in the country, used regularly by more than 90% of the population.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We should note here that in earlier times some people had negative feelings towards the language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: In fact, for many years it was commonly referred to as a broken language, and its use was discouraged.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: But attitudes have changed dramatically.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And today the people of Vanuatu are very proud of this unique language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It is only when we understand the historical context that we can comprehend just why Bishop Palmer developed in Vanuatu.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The first form of pidgin English in this region can be traced to around 1800 when foreign traders arrived and local people were recruited to work as sailors.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: On board multilingual ships, there was an obvious need for a common tongue and pidgin English was born.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: This early former bush llama continued to spread as trade in the Pacific developed in sandalwood and other local commodities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Then from about 1860, a lot of people from Vanuatu traveled to Australia to work on the new plantations as laborers again because of the multilingual nature of these workplaces.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It was very important to have a common language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Finally, in modern times, there have been other pressures that have maintained the need for a common language like many other parts of the world from about the 1950s.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Vanuatu experienced a significant migration of its people from small villages into the city.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And it has been here that Bulama has really established itself as the country's first language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So then how can we describe the language itself?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: In general terms, pidgin languages can be defined as extremely simple versions of the original language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: However, this is not a satisfactory definition in this case, and linguists prefer to describe Bulama as a developed pidgin because it has more rules and ideas than most simple pidgin languages found in other parts of the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Let's think first about the vocabulary, because Britain was a colonial power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The majority of Bellamy's vocabulary is derived from English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: However, some care needs to be taken here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: For example, the word from Belgium can also mean because of.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So we need to be aware that words can have a wider range of meanings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Ambitious drama.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Indeed, there are numerous other potentially misleading terms.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And English is not the only contributor to the vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Again because of the region's history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: There are some words around 5 to 10% that are derived from French.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Then a relatively small number of words have been taken from local Pacific languages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Usually this is the case where there is no English equivalent for naturally occurring phenomena or to describe some aspect of the culture that is unique to the country.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Finally, a word about grammar.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Although the vocabulary is based largely on English, it's important to note that the grammatical structure of llama is derived from patterns common in the local languages of Vanuatu.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Good morning and welcome back to the series of linguistics lectures.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Today I will be talking about the language Bish Llama, which is a form of pidgin English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Linguists use the term pidgin to describe new languages that are created by combining two or more existing languages, often in a simplified form.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: The study of pidgin languages is important because it provides us with information about language change and modification.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: The Pidgin English known as Bish Llama, is used in the South Pacific nation of Vanuatu, a group of islands where 81/1 languages are still regularly used by the local people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: There are a further 17 local languages that are in danger of dying out and eight that have been identified as extinct.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: This gives a total of 106/1 languages in all, a very high number for a small country with a population of just 200,000 people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Then thinking about foreign languages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: English is the most important and has official status, largely because it is the medium for all education purposes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: However, it has been lamented as the most widely spoken language in the country, used regularly by more than 90% of the population.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: We should note here that in earlier times some people had negative feelings towards the language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: In fact, for many years it was commonly referred to as a broken language, and its use was discouraged.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But attitudes have changed dramatically.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And today the people of Vanuatu are very proud of this unique language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It is only when we understand the historical context that we can comprehend just why Bishop Palmer developed in Vanuatu.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: The first form of pidgin English in this region can be traced to around 1800 when foreign traders arrived and local people were recruited to work as sailors.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: On board multilingual ships, there was an obvious need for a common tongue and pidgin English was born.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: This early former bush llama continued to spread as trade in the Pacific developed in sandalwood and other local commodities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Then from about 1860, a lot of people from Vanuatu traveled to Australia to work on the new plantations as laborers again because of the multilingual nature of these workplaces.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It was very important to have a common language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Finally, in modern times, there have been other pressures that have maintained the need for a common language like many other parts of the world from about the 1950s.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Vanuatu experienced a significant migration of its people from small villages into the city.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And it has been here that Bulama has really established itself as the country's first language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So then how can we describe the language itself?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: In general terms, pidgin languages can be defined as extremely simple versions of the original language.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: However, this is not a satisfactory definition in this case, and linguists prefer to describe Bulama as a developed pidgin because it has more rules and ideas than most simple pidgin languages found in other parts of the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Let's think first about the vocabulary, because Britain was a colonial power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: The majority of Bellamy's vocabulary is derived from English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: However, some care needs to be taken here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: For example, the word from Belgium can also mean because of.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So we need to be aware that words can have a wider range of meanings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Ambitious drama.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Indeed, there are numerous other potentially misleading terms.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And English is not the only contributor to the vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Again because of the region's history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: There are some words around 5 to 10% that are derived from French.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Then a relatively small number of words have been taken from local Pacific languages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Usually this is the case where there is no English equivalent for naturally occurring phenomena or to describe some aspect of the culture that is unique to the country.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Finally, a word about grammar.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Although the vocabulary is based largely on English, it's important to note that the grammatical structure of llama is derived from patterns common in the local languages of Vanuatu.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So for example, there are two distinct pronouns meaning we.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: One means I and you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And another means I.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And some others.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But not you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Sounds confusing in English, but in the local languages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Such distinctions are common.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: A different example concerns the word long.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It is almost the only preposition and best lama and may be used in place of a whole range of English words such as at two with on, in and so on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Well, that is the end of the formal part of the lecture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: If you have any questions now, I'll be most happy to.

segments.text: We believe that the first educators of a child are the appearance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We've been looking at marketing techniques which influence buying decisions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Some of these techniques are related to the way the products are presented in the store.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: For supermarkets, the store layout is not as random as it seems.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Decisions have to be made about the arrangement of the aisles where the customers walk and the shelves and so on, where the products are displayed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The most common layout pattern is the grid layout, where parallel aisles are arranged in a rectangular pattern.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Supermarkets like this layout as it allows them to utilize floor space efficiently by providing the greatest amount of display space proportionate to aisle space.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Also, this layout helps to manage traffic flow as it encourages people to all walk in one direction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The main weaknesses of the grid layout are the monotony of rows of aisles and the fact that it is easier for customers to rush through the supermarket without lingering.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Another layout pattern used by supermarkets is known as the free form.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Here, displays and aisles are arranged in a random pattern.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The good thing about this layout is that customers tend to spend more time in the store as they wonder about looking for different products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Its main weakness is the inefficient use of space, which means it is less cost effective.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Then we have the boutique layout where everything is organized around a food specialty such as the bakery.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The advantage of this layout is that it divides parts of the store into smaller areas, which may be distinguished by changes in flooring or displays.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A further advantage is that this style of layout is attractive to shoppers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Space, however, is not used economically and it is therefore expensive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The choice of location of particular types of items in the store is also important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A supermarket's design aims to direct customers to the store's side and rear walls.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Items typically displayed along the rear length of the store include meat and dairy products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Since these appear on the grocery list of the majority of shoppers, this means shoppers must pass by a large number of other items to get to them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Items which consumers tend to spend more time considering before buying, such as cosmetics, are usually placed away from the busy areas so that people can look at them in comfort without feeling rushed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Products placed at the end of aisles are clearly visible, and therefore these locations provide a greater opportunity for shoppers to view the products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Consumers tend to assume that items on display at the end of an aisle are on sale.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But this is often not the case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In fact, supermarket managers often place products which are not selling quickly enough in these positions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The placement of products on shelves is very carefully planned.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Supermarket executives use computer generated plans to help them place products on shelves in a way that ensures consumers spend more on the eye level of the average woman is one meter 60 centimeters off the floor, which is the height of the middle shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the things which cost more are placed here, while cheaper products are placed on higher or lower shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Only items targeted at children break this rule.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They are placed on the lowest shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Supermarkets also use a range of other marketing techniques to encourage consumers to spend more.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's no accident that in nearly every supermarket, the fruit and vegetable department is the first shoppers come to you as they enter the store.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: These, together with flowers, produce a greater profit than any other department.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: After complaints from parents, many supermarkets no longer place popular products aimed at children on the shelves next to the checkout.

segments.transcript: It's important that you attend regularly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: This way you'll get to know other parents well and your child will develop confidence while he or she is here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Younger children might need to leave early.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: It's better to leave early than to go home with an overtired child.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: We do provide drinks for the children, but we ask you to make sure your child has a snack to eat during the morning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: No crisps or chocolate, please.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: I think I'll stop there and ask if anyone's got any questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of section two.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now turn to section three on page four. ------------------------------------------------- Section three, you will hear two sports physiotherapy students called John and Kath preparing a joint presentation on foot injuries in sports players.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26 on page four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I've had a look at your draft presentation plan and compared it with mine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Cath And we seem to have the same basic structure.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: We've both included the same three main sections.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: That's the anatomy of the foot, the injuries and the treatment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And we've organized our presentations in the same way.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But the types of sports we've chosen to illustrate the possible injuries aren't the same.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I'll deal with the anatomy bit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I've got notes and a handout on that from Professor Gilligan's lecture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Oh, I was hoping to do that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I've downloaded some useful stuff.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I do think we should limit this section, though.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: We don't want to spend much time on anatomy when the main focus is on the treatment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: That's true.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: But in the last section, maybe the two of us could show how some of these therapies actually work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I could be the patient.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: And you could do the treatment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Good idea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Because it's hard to find pictures as injuries are mostly internal.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It would be good to hear some firsthand accounts from injured athletes, too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Yeah, but we don't have time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: No.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Should we then discuss different types of heal injury?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It's worth pointing out that these vary enormously in how bad they are.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It might be just a pulled muscle or a bone injury which needs surgery.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Sometimes only an expert can tell the difference.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Excellent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I'll do the slides on that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Leave that one to me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Now, what about causes of heal injuries?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Well, it's easy enough to list them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Overuse improper footwear.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Incorrect running style.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: They're all relevant.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: But for simplicity, let's just pick one cause.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Say stuff about changing your training habits suddenly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: You mean, like, suddenly doing a lot of mountain training?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: That's a good idea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And there was research on that in the latest edition of Physio Journal, wasn't that?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Professor Gilligan recommended it to us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Great.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: And you can leave the bit on stretching techniques to me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I really like all that stuff.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So what's going to be your approach there?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Well, I'll summarize all the various techniques with visual support, and then I'll make the point that the stretching should be carefully managed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Obviously, you have to be careful not to overstretch and to stretch only when your muscles are warmed up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Otherwise, you could do yourself more harm than good.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: It's also important that on a supervised program, stretching is later on, combined with balance exercises which stretch and also strengthen the muscles.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay then.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30 on page five.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It's always useful to have some information on case studies at the end in case we should have material.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Did you manage to find anything?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: A female runner in her thirties talking about her treatment for a swollen heel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Initially, she rested the injury.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: This did help to reduce the swelling, although it was still a little bit uncomfortable.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Then she applied an ice pack to the injury twice a day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Did that work?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Well, she persisted with this treatment for the first month, but decided it wasn't helping.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: After this period, she was shown how to use deep tissue massage techniques and was surprised at how much freedom of movement this created in her foot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Wasn't she having ultrasound treatment?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Yes, she was having sessions at the hospital, but she remained unconvinced about its value as she felt the same about the balancing exercises she was prescribed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay, that's interesting.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I looked at the aftercare program of a male sprinter who was allowed to do some sports activity as part of his rehabilitation after four months of treatment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: He did some light running on grass wearing shoes that gave plenty of support to his injured heel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: So it didn't hurt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Well, he found the heel was sore afterwards and the same happened with some jumping exercises he was asked to try.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Did he go to the gym and use weights?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: After a few weeks and if he used lightweights, he could train without pain.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: He also tried cycling and found this beneficial as his foot was not making contact with the ground.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: He expected a similar result with swimming, but found the repetitive kicking motion was actually aggravating the injury.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Well, both these case studies have value.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of Section three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now turn to section four on page six. ---------------------------------------------- Section four, you will hear part of a lecture on the ways that supermarkets use layout to increase sales.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on pages six and seven.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: We've been looking at marketing techniques which influence buying decisions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Some of these techniques are related to the way the products are presented in the store.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: For supermarkets, the store layout is not as random as it seems.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Decisions have to be made about the arrangement of the aisles where the customers walk and the shelves and so on, where the products are displayed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The most common layout pattern is the grid layout, where parallel aisles are arranged in a rectangular pattern.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Supermarkets like this layout as it allows them to utilize floor space efficiently by providing the greatest amount of display space proportionate to aisle space.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Also, this layout helps to manage traffic flow as it encourages people to all walk in one direction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The main weaknesses of the grid layout are the monotony of rows of aisles and the fact that it is easier for customers to rush through the supermarket without lingering.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Another layout pattern used by supermarkets is known as the free form.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Here, displays and aisles are arranged in a random pattern.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The good thing about this layout is that customers tend to spend more time in the store as they wonder about looking for different products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Its main weakness is the inefficient use of space, which means it is less cost effective.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Then we have the boutique layout where everything is organized around a food specialty such as the bakery.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The advantage of this layout is that it divides parts of the store into smaller areas, which may be distinguished by changes in flooring or displays.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: A further advantage is that this style of layout is attractive to shoppers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Space, however, is not used economically and it is therefore expensive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The choice of location of particular types of items in the store is also important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: A supermarket's design aims to direct customers to the store's side and rear walls.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Items typically displayed along the rear length of the store include meat and dairy products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Since these appear on the grocery list of the majority of shoppers, this means shoppers must pass by a large number of other items to get to them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Items which consumers tend to spend more time considering before buying, such as cosmetics, are usually placed away from the busy areas so that people can look at them in comfort without feeling rushed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Products placed at the end of aisles are clearly visible, and therefore these locations provide a greater opportunity for shoppers to view the products.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Consumers tend to assume that items on display at the end of an aisle are on sale.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: But this is often not the case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: In fact, supermarket managers often place products which are not selling quickly enough in these positions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: The placement of products on shelves is very carefully planned.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Supermarket executives use computer generated plans to help them place products on shelves in a way that ensures consumers spend more on the eye level of the average woman is one meter 60 centimeters off the floor, which is the height of the middle shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: So the things which cost more are placed here, while cheaper products are placed on higher or lower shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Only items targeted at children break this rule.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: They are placed on the lowest shelves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Supermarkets also use a range of other marketing techniques to encourage consumers to spend more.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: It's no accident that in nearly every supermarket, the fruit and vegetable department is the first shoppers come to you as they enter the store.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: These, together with flowers, produce a greater profit than any other department.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: After complaints from parents, many supermarkets no longer place popular products aimed at children on the shelves next to the checkout.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Instead, you are most likely to find products aimed at impulse buyers such as chocolate magazines and other treats.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Many supermarkets have also expanded into non-food areas such as clothing, entertainment and stationery.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: These products often find.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of Section four.

segments.text: Hello.

segments.text: My name's Robert.

segments.text: I've got a four year old daughter called Susie, and I'd like to get some information about your preschool, please.

segments.text: Sure, Robert.

segments.text: Well, Susie's the right age.

segments.text: We take three and four year olds in classes of 20 students.

segments.text: Oh, great.

segments.text: And how many teachers do you have?

segments.text: I'll write that down.

segments.text: Now I know the children attend for two or three days a week.

segments.text: Last year, there seemed to be more of an interest in dancing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The university has decided to enter an international competition next year and we are going to need some enthusiastic undergraduates to help us with the project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The competition is to make an automated vehicle, a kind of robot that will be able to move quickly and accurately on its own.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: All the vehicles will then enter a race which will take place here in the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: So the engineering school will be collaborating with the computer science department and possibly the Automotive Design Department, although that's yet to be confirmed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What they have to do is try to design an automated vehicle which will be able to complete the course.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: To give you an idea of how tough this race is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: One vehicle last year only managed 12 kilometers of the 280 kilometers stretch of California desert that forms the racetrack.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The vehicles in the race must cover the whole distance without a human driver and quite autonomously identify and steer around corners and avoid unexpected hazards.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Things like rocks, for example.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It's a challenging task because there are lots of obstacles of this kind along the route.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: As I said in last year's event, the most successful vehicle only drove 12 kilometers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Then its team decided to deactivate it because it had gotten too near a cliff in the race held earlier this year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: There still wasn't a winner, but they did much better.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And there was one design which we will be analyzing carefully in seminars.

segments.text: Its strength was in its onboard technology.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That particular vehicle built a three dimensional picture of its surroundings using video cameras and lasers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It was equipped with seven laptop computers, which analyze the incoming information ten times a second, and it drove along at a comfortable 55 kilometers per hour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The design details have been published, so we hope to learn from them and go on to make ours even better for next year's competition.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The competition is open to all universities and there's a prize of $2 million for the winner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: But it's really about more than that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The sponsors are hoping to see innovative design ideas that they can transfer into commercial production.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: You'll get a lot out of this project as well in terms of working as a team and broadening your knowledge of the subject.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The key to winning is unlikely to be anything to do with what the vehicle looks like.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Programing skills will decide who eventually wins first prize.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4

segments.text: I'll be handing out some scientific reports about this year's vehicle shortly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So the teachers are doing a lot of activities related to that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Last year, there seemed to be more of an interest in dancing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Well, Susie would love either of those.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The teachers may sometimes play quiet games with the children, but we always make time for a story each day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's a very important part of the program here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes, of course.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10 on page two.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Now I'd like to ask you about the fees, if that's okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Sure.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: We actually had to put them up this term, I'm afraid.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I heard from a friend of mine that it used to be $420 for the term, but it's just gone up to $470.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Is that right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Yes, we had to add the extra $50 to cover costs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Things got a lot more expensive last year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I understand.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And I think the fees are still quite reasonable.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Another school I've spoken to charge $500 per term.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: My friend also told me that his daughter went on a trip to the local zoo and that the cost of that was covered in the fees.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Is that right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Yes, we did that last year, but will be going to a farm this year instead.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: We vary it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So for example, we may go to the theater next year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It sounds like fun.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Also included in the price is membership of a special library.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Children can borrow a toy and keep it for a week and choose a different one the following week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's very popular.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: What a great idea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: We would certainly make use of that system if we enroll.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Now, is there anything else I should know?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, the children have arrested during the day, and we make up a little bed for them with sheets and blankets.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But we advise parents to pack a pillow in the child's bag as we don't provide one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay, I'll make a note of that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So what should I do if I want to come and look around the school during the day and meet the staff?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The best thing is to call the teacher on the classroom mobile and she'll tell you which time is best to visit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Shall I give you the number?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes, please.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Thanks for all your help, Sally.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And we hope to see you soon.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: No problem.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Bye for now.

segments.transcript: That is the end of Section one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

segments.transcript: Now turn to section two on page three. ----------------------------------------- Section two, you will hear part of a talk about how students can get help finding a part time job while they're studying.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15 on page three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Hi.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Thanks for coming along.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: My name is Marissa, and I'm going to tell you a bit about finding part time jobs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Not everybody wants to work when they're studying.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And as this is your first year, you may feel that you've quite enough to do as it is, but you may change your mind or find that you need to earn some extra cash.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: However, if you are a student from overseas, there may be particular conditions attached to working in this country.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So you should check with the staff at the center before applying for a job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Right now, the university has its own job center on the campus.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, actually, it's not on this main Helston campus.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's based in the student services building on the campus called Woodside, spelled w0odsi.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: D e.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The center works on a drop in basis, which means that you don't have to make an appointment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's open six days a week, Monday to Saturday and 9 hours a day from ten in the morning until eight at night.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The center is run by other students, but a professional employment lawyer is on hand every Tuesday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: If you want any advice about your job, there may be a queue, in which case you will have to wait.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So make sure you allow plenty of time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Part time jobs become available almost every day and they are advertised on the university website, which you can access through the library.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: If the computer center is closed, you should check things daily and if you see a job which interests you, call in at the center.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20 on page four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: There's a good variety of jobs on offer in the university itself just now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: For example, they're looking for people to check that all the vehicles using the university car parks have got up to date permits.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Office jobs rarely come up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But in future, the university is hoping to be able to offer jobs in the city center.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: There are also recruitment open days, which are held regularly during the year when local employers come into the university to recruit students for part time work within their company.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: These two day events are scheduled well in advance each term and are advertised in the usual places.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Of course, part time work is useful to supplement your income, but it's also a valuable way of building up an employment record that reflects your skills and capabilities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: One of the most common complaints of graduates leaving university is that many jobs require proven experience.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So those applicants who have evidence of part time work on their CV often have an advantage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The job center advertises jobs, which will give you skills such as using word processing packages, spreadsheets or supervisory skills.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So if you have to work, use the opportunity to develop skills which will help you secure a job in the future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Now, what about the financial side of things?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, students who work part time can no longer expect to be paid cash.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: An employer will deduct tax from what you earn.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But depending on your own individual circumstances and how much you earn in a year, you should be able to reclaim some of this.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You may also have to contribute towards an insurance scheme, but you must ask your employer about these deductions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You should also check whether you will be paid weekly or monthly, and if you work extra hours, what your overtime rate will be.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's also necessary to make sure that your employer knows that you may only be able to work during term time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Communication between you and your employer is very important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But don't expect all employers to use email.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: If you are ill or cannot get into work for whatever reason, make sure your employer knows in good time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: That shouldn't be a problem now that everyone has a mobile phone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And if you decide to leave the job, you should make sure you put this in writing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Some employers require a month's notice, even for a part time job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So what sort of work can you expect to find?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, as I said earlier, there is a.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of section two.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now turn to section three on page five. ----------------------------------------- Section three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You will hear a sociology student called John discussing his research project about the use of public services with his tutor.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26 on page five.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Hello, John.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Come in and sit down.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You here to discuss your research project, are you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I've more or less decided what to do, but I'd like your opinion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Fine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You've chosen a topic?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I want to look at how people use public services in their local area.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Things like parks and swimming pools.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, the kind of information you'll get is very useful for town planning, of course.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Do you have a special interest in public services?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Not really.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It's just that I found a report in the college library about an investigation that was done ten years ago, and I thought it would be interesting to do a parallel one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Ten years is a relatively short space of time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What do you expect to find?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Do you think things will be more or less the same as before?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I think there'll be some differences.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: For example, I think the number of people going to the library will have decreased.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And I'd guess that older people are using the sports center more often than they used to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Fine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So those are your hypotheses now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What sort of data are you going to use?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I was thinking of using official records from the managements or the local council and analyzing them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: They should be easy to obtain.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I don't think that source of information would be confidential.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Yes, you're probably right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: There might not be as much information as you'd like, but it'd certainly be the easiest kind of data to work with a bit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Have you considered using a questionnaire as well?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It's okay to get data from more than one source.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It's a bonus.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You've already done the module on questionnaire design, haven't you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And it'll be good to get experience, because next year you'll have to do something similar for your final dissertation on a bigger scale.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And what are the variables you'll be looking at?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Are you going to look at people's level of education, whether they have a degree, for example?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I hadn't planned to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Do you think I should?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, you might see some interesting patterns.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And that'll tie in nicely with my plans to analyze the kind of work people do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What about the size of your sample?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Have you got any thoughts on the number of questionnaires you might send out?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: The previous study surveyed 120 people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I don't think I can really analyze more than 50 working by myself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: So I should probably distribute about 80 questionnaires altogether to allow for wastage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Do you think that's enough?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Definitely.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: I know that your project guidelines recommend a minimum of 100, but that's an ideal number, and you're working by yourself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And anyway, this assignment is mainly about giving you practice in research methods.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30 on page six.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And think of ways you can encourage people to actually complete the questionnaire, for example, to make sure that your questions make sense.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: You should try them out beforehand.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay, that's no problem.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: My friends will help.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Good.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Sometimes you get unpredicted responses and you have to rephrase the question.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And I know that you usually get a better return if you deliver questionnaires in person.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But there will be too many.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But I could enclose a stamps envelope for the return post.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: It's a bit expensive, but I think it'd be worth it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Good.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Some people say that another way of increasing returns is to make the questionnaires anonymous.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But usually people put their names on anyway, so I don't think that would make much difference.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And can you give me a bit more advice about the questionnaire?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Would it be a good idea to have a short paragraph at the top explaining what I'm doing and why?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Definitely.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And don't forget, you'll need to get a bit of information about your subjects, what age group they're in, and perhaps how long they've lived in the area.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So you'll need questions for that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Yes, I suppose that will mean it takes a bit longer to complete.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: But should I give them my phone number in case there's anything they're not sure about?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: I wouldn't if I were, you know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: And do I have to use open ended questions as well as closed questions?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: I know the books say it's better to have a mixture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, it depends.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In this case, I'd stick to closed questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The results will be much more manageable like that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: If I drive some questions tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.transcript: Would it be okay to bring them to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of Section three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You will hear a tutor talking to a group of students about a project to build a driverless vehicle.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on pages seven and eight.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Hello, everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I have an exciting announcement to make.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The university has decided to enter an international competition next year and we are going to need some enthusiastic undergraduates to help us with the project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The competition is to make an automated vehicle, a kind of robot that will be able to move quickly and accurately on its own.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: All the vehicles will then enter a race which will take place here in the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: So the engineering school will be collaborating with the computer science department and possibly the Automotive Design Department, although that's yet to be confirmed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: What they have to do is try to design an automated vehicle which will be able to complete the course.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: To give you an idea of how tough this race is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: One vehicle last year only managed 12 kilometers of the 280 kilometers stretch of California desert that forms the racetrack.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The vehicles in the race must cover the whole distance without a human driver and quite autonomously identify and steer around corners and avoid unexpected hazards.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Things like rocks, for example.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: It's a challenging task because there are lots of obstacles of this kind along the route.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: As I said in last year's event, the most successful vehicle only drove 12 kilometers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Then its team decided to deactivate it because it had gotten too near a cliff in the race held earlier this year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: There still wasn't a winner, but they did much better.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: And there was one design which we will be analyzing carefully in seminars.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Its strength was in its onboard technology.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: That particular vehicle built a three dimensional picture of its surroundings using video cameras and lasers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: It was equipped with seven laptop computers, which analyze the incoming information ten times a second, and it drove along at a comfortable 55 kilometers per hour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The design details have been published, so we hope to learn from them and go on to make ours even better for next year's competition.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The competition is open to all universities and there's a prize of $2 million for the winner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: But it's really about more than that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The sponsors are hoping to see innovative design ideas that they can transfer into commercial production.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: You'll get a lot out of this project as well in terms of working as a team and broadening your knowledge of the subject.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The key to winning is unlikely to be anything to do with what the vehicle looks like.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Programing skills will decide who eventually wins first prize.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: The design will need technological expertize in this area above all, and that's what the team who work on the project will need to focus on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: I'll be handing out some scientific reports about this year's vehicle shortly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: It's interesting to read that even after months and months of planning, building and trials, many of the teams were amazed that the vehicles did what they wanted them to do at all because so many things can go wrong on the day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: So even though no vehicle actually completed the course, they were pleased they got as far as they did.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: If any of you are interested, this is the plan of action.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Keep an eye on the main noticeboard for details.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Firstly, at the beginning of May, we'll be scheduling a seminar to introduce the project to anyone who might be interested.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Later in the month, we'll be asking you to submit a short essay, letting us know why you feel you should be chosen to take part in the project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: You'll need to tell us about any particular skills that you have and can bring to the team and any experience you may have had in the field.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Then in June, we're organizing a trip to a factory to chat over some design considerations with specialists there who have kindly agreed to act as consultants throughout the project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Then, at the beginning of the next semester in September, we thought we'd hold a weekend workshop to share ideas and see computer aided design demonstrations.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: We have a brand new package which sponsors have kindly financed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: You'll need to be able to use it with confidence before we start.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: In December, we'll be asking you to submit your outline designs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: And the following month will choose the team and start work in earnest.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: It sounds like a lot of fun, but it will also require serious commitment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: So please think this through carefully.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Some handouts are coming around now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.transcript: Any questions?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of Section four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of the listening test.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have 10 minutes to transfer your answers to the listening answer sheet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You have 2 minutes left.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You have one minute left.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Please stop writing and wait for your question booklet to be collected.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Today, I'm going to be talking about the first year of a regeneration project in a mangrove forest.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Mangrove forests are found along river estuaries and coastlines and are important because they prevent flooding by acting as a barrier between the land and sea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The mangrove trees have special roots which can breathe and allow them to survive in thick, airless mud.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They are also a very important habitat for wading birds, fish and other animals in the area where the project is taking place.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There have been a number of problems since the area was first settled over 100 years ago.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Many of the mangrove trees were initially burnt as firewood by local farmers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The mangrove forests were also poisoned by settlers farming methods because the farmers used fertilizer to increase crop yields.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And this started to seep into the water, eventually killing part of the mangrove forest.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Farming in the area wasn't successful, and what was left of the mangrove forest area wasn't valued by local people as crops couldn't be grown there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so what happened was that the area started to be used as somewhere to dump trash.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Action was urgently needed to protect the mangrove forest and prevent flooding.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so the mangrove regeneration project was set up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The conservationists involved decided to construct a sand barrier around the forests, but unfortunately this proved to be ineffective.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The only way forward appeared to be to grow new mangroves from seed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Several species of mangrove inhabit the forests in this area of the United States.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But it is the gray mangroves that we are concerned with here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The seed of this plant is about the size of an almond, and most seeds fall only when they are fully ripe.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The Mangrove Regeneration Project first began three years ago.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The first set of seedlings was planted in small plots and left to germinate in a hothouse.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The plants thrived and large roots appeared at the bottom of the pots.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Ideally, these seedlings should have been conditioned with increasingly salty water before being planted in the sea.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They had, in fact only been watered with rainwater as the plants weren't used to a saline environment.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It was decided to plant them out on the south side of a small island nearby.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It was hoped that this would allow them to get used to salt water gradually.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Since this part of the island was flooded every day at high tide, there were over 100 plants planted in this particular spot, and it was necessary to protect them not from the large number of wading birds which visit the area looking for food, but from the large rabbit colony living in the area.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The process for the second set of seedlings was completely different.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Young seedlings were collected from the forests and then taken to a new site.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The seedlings were then planted in the seabed behind old mangrove roots for protection.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: However, this method did not prove very successful, and the vast majority of these seedlings were washed away in a storm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Luckily, the first set of seedlings survived, and this method is the one which the project will continue to use in the future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now I'd like to describe in more detail the process.
