segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For today's session, we're going to look at the job market and employer's hiring strategies.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It mainly takes great people to generate and execute efficient strategies and ideas.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In fact, a company's growth is strongly supported by its human resources.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Therefore, we'll look at the determining factors for recruitment, the traits of a successful applicant, and the possible reasons for rejection.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: First, let's take a look at the job market for students who have just graduated from secondary schools.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what should they focus on when applying for a job?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is education the most important factor in recruitment?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, actually, the degree is not that important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's not the only factor that personal managers take into consideration.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Some employees with years of work experience still have a competitive edge over fresh graduates with a higher educational degree.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, with neither an impressive educational background nor practical experience, secondary school graduates should stress that they have great enthusiasm for work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Employees who are interested in their job often work hard and are willing to take more responsibilities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What else should they highlight during a job interview?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, it is wise for them to demonstrate that they possess valuable characteristics such as curiosity, willingness to learn new stuff and good interpersonal skills.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Companies favor applicants who are easygoing and fit in quickly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But I guess things get harder for women to reenter the workforce and reconnect after raising children at home.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: After taking an extended absence from work, women with young children have to strike a good balance between work and family.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Changes have to be made within the family to ensure they have sufficient working hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Apart from that, they are working with a totally new colleague in an unfamiliar workplace.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: After even two or three years of absence, they face challenges of rusty or obsolete skills.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Even though they are quite confident in themselves, they often find it hard to adapt to these changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But on the other hand, many employers find these mature women valuable assets in the workplace.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They are excellent role models for younger employees as being quite motivated and with strong work ethic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Indeed, employers not only need qualified, but also flexible and well-trained employees.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Given the experience, perspectives and stability, these women are offered unique opportunities in today's workplace.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes, exactly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what kind of people do companies generally find unwelcoming?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Will they consider candidates from a rival company?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, actually, hiring employees from a competing firm is not a taboo.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Highly skilled workers are always welcomed, no matter where they're from.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What concerns employers the most is how they left the previous company that they had worked for years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If they have been fired.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They must have done something wrong during the previous job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What about people who remain unemployed for a considerable period of time?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, this type of employee isn't at the bottom of the employment list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The reason why they remain unemployed is the key.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Most companies cast doubts on applicants who left the job simply because they didn't like the working hours or the work assigned.

segments.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Have you read any articles about worker retrenchment?

segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Worker retrenchment on a massive scale is sometimes introduced as one of the short term measures to resuscitate the industry through the reduction of overhead costs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Workers are also laid off as companies restructure and reform.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But what happens to these retrenched workers afterwards?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is it easy for them to find another job?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, generally companies are reluctant to hire them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Why is that?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They must have plenty of work experience in the previous industry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Isn't that a strength for them in the job market?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Actually, new industries are eager to hire experienced workers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But retrenched workers know nothing about other industries.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And it also costs employers more to retrain them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They need training courses to acquire relevant skills and qualifications for a new career.

segments.text: Our government is providing public training programs to help them identify their current skills and acquire new skills to improve their career options.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Isn't that right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But retrenched workers are generally too old.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They are less motivated and energized at work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Companies thus prefer younger employees to them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They are also reluctant to adjust and are unwilling to be retrained to retrench.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Workers from companies with big names have an advantage over other job applicants.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No employers today value skills more than where they're previously from.

segments.text: Right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what are the most common factors of rejection during application?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Applicants are rejected mainly for three reasons.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: First, they have experience and skills that are irrelevant to the industry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Even experienced workers may receive rejection letters wearing appropriate clothes, and how they look during an interview are key to a successful interview.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No matter how good their presentation skills are, a shirt with stains or informal clothes like a pair of jeans only means the applicants aren't taking the interview seriously.

segments.text: Yes, during an interview, formal dress is key to a good start and will inevitably affect how people evaluate you later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What's the third factor?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let me guess.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is it interpersonal skills?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Companies are eager to hire people who can work well with others and fit in quickly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's difficult to work in an environment full of conflicts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Therefore, people who don't get along well with others are often rejected.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1

segments.text: Four. ------------------------------------------------------ You will hear part of a lecture on organic farming.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: First, you have some time to look at questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hi, everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What I'm going to talk about today is organic farming.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Let's first look at what organic farming is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It can be defined as one or more systems of production which don't use synthetic fertilizers, manmade pesticides, herbicides, antibiotics or livestock feed additives to grow crops and raise animals.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Virtually all organic farmers prefer to use renewable resources and recycling to give what conventional farmers might consider a waste back to the soil of Mother Nature.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: From this we can see organic farming is a sustainable production system, which is one of its advantages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Organic farmers use numerous techniques to promote the quality of life of plants and animals within existing ecosystems and minimize pollution that occurs with all conventional farming practices.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Another benefit is that with the increasing consumer demand for a healthier, more nutritionally balanced product, the sales of organically produced food are promoted.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: According to the research, it has become the fastest growing sector of agriculture and has shown an annual increase of at least 20% during the last six years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What's more, both chemical fertilizers and synthetic pesticides consume nonrenewable resources such as oil and coal.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But the development of organic farming can lower the demand for these fertilizers and pesticides, so it is conducive to the conservation of essential energy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: At the same time, it also can reduce industrial pollution caused by the production of these chemical substances.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Organic farming differs greatly from the traditional one in a number of ways.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Let's discuss it from the perspective of agricultural biodiversity.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Firstly, for instance, earthworms are an important indicator of soil fertility.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Studies have shown that the density and species number of earthworms in organically managed soils are three times as high as those in conventional fields.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Moreover, the biodiversity in organic farming can also be reflected in the number of insects, which is twice as many as those in traditional farms.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: This might be highly related to the fact that organic vegetables are grown without any human made pesticides, making these vegetables more likely to be damaged.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The other main difference between organic and traditional farming lies in crop yields.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: One of the biggest concerns of organic farmers organic farms, though possibly well adapted for certain local environments, produce less food per unit of land.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For example, organic vegetables like tomatoes and potatoes yielded 40% less than conventional ones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In addition, research has also found the number of weeds produced in winter is about 90% at present, which is decreased by 10% than before.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, lower crop yields in organic farming are still inevitable at the moment anyway.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Organic farming is a new direction for agricultural development.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: These days, a variety of organic products are cultivated not only for humans, but also for animals.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For example, organic grass is commonly used in organic farms to feed cows.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because of the nonuse of synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, it can protect cows from diseases brought by large scale breeding, thus ensuring the quality of raw milk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But an interesting phenomenon is that its production has remained constant these years, which is quite unique compared with other types of crops.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Research on organic farming has covered various aspects and involved many countries.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: According to one study, organic farming was proposed in India in the early 1960s when it was faced with acute shortages of food grains due to the ever increasing population and natural disasters.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Although it could not be applied successfully at first, as farmers had been familiar with conventional instructions, proponents of organic farming claimed that organic agriculture emphasized biodiversity and effective soil management could enhance the capacity to mitigate and even reverse the effects of climate change.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So India needed organic farming along with modern scientific agriculture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The study shows that in 2006, India became the country with the largest number of organic products and the production of crops kept growing year on year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Another international review about organic farming presents.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In the first part, the people today have become increasingly interested in organic food and this opinion is quite the same as that of other articles.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But what impressed me most was the volume of the investigation the author did in different countries.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: He conducted a survey in 99 countries, of which 66 are convinced that organic farming is beneficial to animals, while eight hold the opposite opinion and the remaining 25 say it is inconclusive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Therefore, the last part of the review is mainly talking about whether organic farming brings positive effects to animals.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We can see there are different views about the advantages of organic farming.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Some may think it can provide more nutritious and healthier food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Others may say it can protect the natural environment and benefit wildlife.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, as far as I'm concerned, it's you, the ones who buy organic products that will decide what they can bring to you because market demand determines everything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, that's all I want to say.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Now, let's open it up for discussion.

segments.text: That is the end of part four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Hi, everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What I'm going to talk about today is organic farming.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Let's first look at what organic farming is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It can be defined as one or more systems of production which don't use synthetic fertilizers, manmade pesticides, herbicides, antibiotics or livestock feed additives to grow crops and raise animals.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Virtually all organic farmers prefer to use renewable resources and recycling to give what conventional farmers might consider a waste back to the soil of Mother Nature.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: From this we can see organic farming is a sustainable production system, which is one of its advantages.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Organic farmers use numerous techniques to promote the quality of life of plants and animals within existing ecosystems and minimize pollution that occurs with all conventional farming practices.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Another benefit is that with the increasing consumer demand for a healthier, more nutritionally balanced product, the sales of organically produced food are promoted.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: According to the research, it has become the fastest growing sector of agriculture and has shown an annual increase of at least 20% during the last six years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What's more, both chemical fertilizers and synthetic pesticides consume nonrenewable resources such as oil and coal.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But the development of organic farming can lower the demand for these fertilizers and pesticides, so it is conducive to the conservation of essential energy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: At the same time, it also can reduce industrial pollution caused by the production of these chemical substances.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Organic farming differs greatly from the traditional one in a number of ways.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Let's discuss it from the perspective of agricultural biodiversity.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Firstly, for instance, earthworms are an important indicator of soil fertility.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Studies have shown that the density and species number of earthworms in organically managed soils are three times as high as those in conventional fields.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Moreover, the biodiversity in organic farming can also be reflected in the number of insects, which is twice as many as those in traditional farms.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: This might be highly related to the fact that organic vegetables are grown without any human made pesticides, making these vegetables more likely to be damaged.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The other main difference between organic and traditional farming lies in crop yields.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: One of the biggest concerns of organic farmers organic farms, though possibly well adapted for certain local environments, produce less food per unit of land.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: For example, organic vegetables like tomatoes and potatoes yielded 40% less than conventional ones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In addition, research has also found the number of weeds produced in winter is about 90% at present, which is decreased by 10% than before.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: However, lower crop yields in organic farming are still inevitable at the moment anyway.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Organic farming is a new direction for agricultural development.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: These days, a variety of organic products are cultivated not only for humans, but also for animals.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: For example, organic grass is commonly used in organic farms to feed cows.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Because of the nonuse of synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, it can protect cows from diseases brought by large scale breeding, thus ensuring the quality of raw milk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But an interesting phenomenon is that its production has remained constant these years, which is quite unique compared with other types of crops.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Research on organic farming has covered various aspects and involved many countries.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: According to one study, organic farming was proposed in India in the early 1960s when it was faced with acute shortages of food grains due to the ever increasing population and natural disasters.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Although it could not be applied successfully at first, as farmers had been familiar with conventional instructions, proponents of organic farming claimed that organic agriculture emphasized biodiversity and effective soil management could enhance the capacity to mitigate and even reverse the effects of climate change.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So India needed organic farming along with modern scientific agriculture.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The study shows that in 2006, India became the country with the largest number of organic products and the production of crops kept growing year on year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Another international review about organic farming presents.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In the first part, the people today have become increasingly interested in organic food and this opinion is quite the same as that of other articles.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But what impressed me most was the volume of the investigation the author did in different countries.

segments.transcript: He conducted a survey in 99 countries, of which 66 are convinced that organic farming is beneficial to animals, while eight hold the opposite opinion and the remaining 25 say it is inconclusive.

segments.text: You will hear a traffic police officer talking to a group of listeners about driving license application and traffic conditions in the UK.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hello.

segments.text: I'm Edward, and I'm here to tell you about road conditions in various areas of the UK.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I am also going to tell you about driver's licenses in the UK.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you have never had a driver's license or you have one from another country and you want to get a UK license, you must be a UK resident.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: You will need to show a medical report when your UK license needs to be renewed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you are trying to translate your original foreign driving license to apply for a UK license, which is a must if you want to be able to drive here, you will need to visit an official agency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: These are scattered throughout the London area and are well equipped to assist you with any questions you might have and any services they offer are included in your license fee.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you already have a translated license but need some personal information updating, you do not need to pay for the update.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They'll do it for free when you are getting a new driving license.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: You may need to have a new photo taken as some photos are rejected.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's actually okay if your photo is too small since we can get it enlarged with our printer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The majority of rejected photos are the ones that were taken with a cream backdrop instead of a monotone gray background.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We've now found that photos with the latter allow us to identify the license holder much more easily.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you were wearing glasses on the previous photo, you don't need to worry about it since it is still allowed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If you are not sure whether your previous license is still valid, then the license checking service is for you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The procedures are quite clear and you just have to follow them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Ideally, I would like to see the process going faster since it can take hours to finish.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: From my standpoint, it will help.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: If all the applicants bring the necessary ID with them, then all they have to do is just fill in the forms accordingly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Step by step, I'm often asked whether I have a personal recommendation about the fastest or cheapest place to get all this done.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But I think it really depends on where you are.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They can all get busy at some point and when it is quiet at one branch, it may be busy in another.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So take your pick.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: All I would say is that there is absolutely no difference in price.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's a standard fee.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The only advice I would give is that the quickest way to complete an application is to fill out the form on the Internet and then bring a print copy with you to the agency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Location of your choice.

segments.text: Next.

segments.text: People frequently ask me what I think of the road conditions in some of our cities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: London is obviously the biggest and busiest and there are lots of parking restrictions, one way systems and so on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But on the whole, I find the traffic signs are very clear.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In Edinburgh, most people use digital maps to get to know local traffic and road conditions, which can be estimated through different traffic flow lines.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It is a city of lights, traffic lights, but they are extremely efficient as their timed perfectly to get the traffic flowing smoothly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's important because pedestrian areas and crossings are always packed with people on foot, which needs strong regulation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The city of Cardiff has tackled traffic flow in a different way.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It recently completed a road expansion scheme and the extra lanes of the dual carriageway are easing congestion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It's a similar story in Manchester.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Instead of going through the town center, most vehicles choose ring roads so as to avoid the downtown congestion.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It can still happen, though, so there's a possibility that the city will introduce checkpoints where the police can intervene to direct traffic at peak periods.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And finally, they say all roads lead to Rome.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And you could say that about Oxford.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I like the many options for getting in and out of the city because drivers can always find alternative routes.

segments.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part three. -------------------------------------------------- Part four, you will hear part of a presentation about the early history of salt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In my presentation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm going to talk about salt in modern times when we talk about salt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: People may associate it with high blood pressure or increased heart risk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And many health experts warn that we should use less salt in our meals and dishes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, we should not ignore its importance in our cuisine and even in early human history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Salt is one of the oldest, most ubiquitous food seasonings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The taste of salt is one of the basic human tastes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: More importantly, salt plays an indispensable role in the health of human beings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For example, it regulates the body's acid base balance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Because of its importance to survival, salt has often been considered a valuable commodity during human history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: This can be tracked all the way back to ancient Greece, ancient Egypt and ancient Rome, when salt was highly valued and used as a method of trade and currency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In ancient Rome, the busiest road leading to the city was the Via Solaria, which means the salt route in English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: A soldier's pay, which partly consisted of salt, was known as salary magenta in Latin, from which we derived the English word salary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: A soldier salary was cut if he was not worth his salt, an expression still used today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In fact, salt was not only the first condiment discovered, but also the first preservative.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We know today that food goes bad because micro-organisms in the food multiply in abundance and a high salt environment is not conducive to microbial reproduction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Extremely high concentrations of salt can even kill microorganisms in the food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The ancients certainly didn't know this, but they did know that salted food can be preserved for a long time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The use of salt as a preservative can be traced to ancient Sweden.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: At first, hunting was the principal means of livelihood.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In this case, meat supplies were unlikely to be frequent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What's more, fewer animals were available for hunting in order to ensure the supply of meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Many families in Sweden began to raise animals in the surrounding forests during the summer, when the weather was suitable for animals to survive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: These animals were fed every day until about 3 to 4 months later that in October they were ready to be butchered for meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And that was the only month when ancient Swedish people had fresh meat on their table.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then, with the continuous increase in productivity, people finally had some meat left.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, how to store the meat had become a headache until someone invented a whole new way to preserve food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Salting people tried to keep meat from going bad by adding some salt to it, and it could be preserved for several months and even years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: There was evidence that salt was widely used to preserve meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Historical documents in 1573 recorded the Swedish King's Everyday meals, mentioning that £175 of meat was consumed each year, but over £150 was salty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: From this, we can clearly see the importance of salt in Sweden at that time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: In addition, the documents also noted the annual sales of beer in Sweden soared during that period and this must be related to high levels of salt in their food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Now let's turn to the sources of salt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Where is salt from?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Well, salt is common in nature.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It has long been found that salt can be extracted from seawater, mineral deposits, saline, lakes, brine, spring, etc., among which the two most important ones are oceans and basins.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: On the floor of the latter often lie deserts where traces of salt can be found, such as the Sahara.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Furthermore, the quality of different salt types varies a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For example, salt from seawater is always mixed with impurities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So after the salt is dried, the sediments and other chemicals need to be purified before eating.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, this is not the case with salt from springwater.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We can hardly find any impurities and the salt level is much more concentrated.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then how did people distribute salt around the world?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Of course, in modern times we have various ways of transporting goods.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But in ancient times, it was not the case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Take ancient Sweden we mentioned before as an example because of the heavy use of salt in the diet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sweden could not feed itself and had to import large amounts of salt from other countries in order to make sure they could buy enough salt from abroad.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The Swedish had to attach great importance to shipping and keep it undamaged as it was the most crucial way at that time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: While in other ancient countries, in order to distribute salt to other places, groups of men were employed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They put bags of salt on their shoulders or backs and moved them to the surrounding regions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And gradually these people were considered as a mode of transport in early times.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Later, with the improvement of traffic conditions, salt trade between different regions was boosted and long distance food trade was also promoted.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Making communication between different cultures more frequent and.

segments.transcript: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: Now listen carefully and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In my presentation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: I'm going to talk about salt in modern times when we talk about salt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: People may associate it with high blood pressure or increased heart risk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And many health experts warn that we should use less salt in our meals and dishes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: However, we should not ignore its importance in our cuisine and even in early human history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Salt is one of the oldest, most ubiquitous food seasonings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The taste of salt is one of the basic human tastes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: More importantly, salt plays an indispensable role in the health of human beings.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: For example, it regulates the body's acid base balance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Because of its importance to survival, salt has often been considered a valuable commodity during human history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: This can be tracked all the way back to ancient Greece, ancient Egypt and ancient Rome, when salt was highly valued and used as a method of trade and currency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In ancient Rome, the busiest road leading to the city was the Via Solaria, which means the salt route in English.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: A soldier's pay, which partly consisted of salt, was known as salary magenta in Latin, from which we derived the English word salary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: A soldier salary was cut if he was not worth his salt, an expression still used today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In fact, salt was not only the first condiment discovered, but also the first preservative.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: We know today that food goes bad because micro-organisms in the food multiply in abundance and a high salt environment is not conducive to microbial reproduction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Extremely high concentrations of salt can even kill microorganisms in the food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The ancients certainly didn't know this, but they did know that salted food can be preserved for a long time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The use of salt as a preservative can be traced to ancient Sweden.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: At first, hunting was the principal means of livelihood.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In this case, meat supplies were unlikely to be frequent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: What's more, fewer animals were available for hunting in order to ensure the supply of meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Many families in Sweden began to raise animals in the surrounding forests during the summer, when the weather was suitable for animals to survive.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: These animals were fed every day until about 3 to 4 months later that in October they were ready to be butchered for meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And that was the only month when ancient Swedish people had fresh meat on their table.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Then, with the continuous increase in productivity, people finally had some meat left.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: However, how to store the meat had become a headache until someone invented a whole new way to preserve food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Salting people tried to keep meat from going bad by adding some salt to it, and it could be preserved for several months and even years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: There was evidence that salt was widely used to preserve meat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Historical documents in 1573 recorded the Swedish King's Everyday meals, mentioning that £175 of meat was consumed each year, but over £150 was salty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: From this, we can clearly see the importance of salt in Sweden at that time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: In addition, the documents also noted the annual sales of beer in Sweden soared during that period and this must be related to high levels of salt in their food.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Now let's turn to the sources of salt.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Where is salt from?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Well, salt is common in nature.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: It has long been found that salt can be extracted from seawater, mineral deposits, saline, lakes, brine, spring, etc., among which the two most important ones are oceans and basins.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: On the floor of the latter often lie deserts where traces of salt can be found, such as the Sahara.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Furthermore, the quality of different salt types varies a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: For example, salt from seawater is always mixed with impurities.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: So after the salt is dried, the sediments and other chemicals need to be purified before eating.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: However, this is not the case with salt from springwater.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: We can hardly find any impurities and the salt level is much more concentrated.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Then how did people distribute salt around the world?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Of course, in modern times we have various ways of transporting goods.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: But in ancient times, it was not the case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Take ancient Sweden we mentioned before as an example because of the heavy use of salt in the diet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Sweden could not feed itself and had to import large amounts of salt from other countries in order to make sure they could buy enough salt from abroad.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: The Swedish had to attach great importance to shipping and keep it undamaged as it was the most crucial way at that time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: While in other ancient countries, in order to distribute salt to other places, groups of men were employed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: They put bags of salt on their shoulders or backs and moved them to the surrounding regions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: And gradually these people were considered as a mode of transport in early times.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Later, with the improvement of traffic conditions, salt trade between different regions was boosted and long distance food trade was also promoted.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.transcript: Making communication between different cultures more frequent and.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: That is the end of part four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.transcript: You now have one minute to check.

paragraphs.text: Tuatara are lizard-like reptiles, found only in New Zealand. They are representative of ancient life forms. Tuatara are the only living representatives of an ancient lineage of reptiles called Sphenodontia, which is over 250 million years old. Because tuatara still look like fossils of reptiles that lived during the age of dinosaurs, they are often called living fossils. Now just two species of tuatara survive, and only in New Zealand. One is the Brothers Island tuatara which, until recent re-introductions to sanctuaries (safe places for wildlife), only survived on North Brother Island. The other species is the common tuatara, which survives on many other offshore islands. Although the tuatara species appear similar, they have genetic differences. Tuatara bones have been found in many parts of New Zealand. Where dated, they are usually a few hundred to 5,000 years old. It is not known whether these bones are from the two living species or other species that are now extinct.

Many anatomical features distinguish tuatara from other living reptiles - for example, they have a defining pattern of openings in the skull and a unique type of hemoglobin in the blood, and males have no external reproductive organ. Adults are between 30 and 75 centimetres long, and weigh between 250 and 1.200 grams. Males are larger than females, and have more developed spines in the crest along the neck, back and tail.

The male tuatara courts the female by approaching her with a proud walk. Tuatara mate in late summer, and the female usually lays 6-10 eggs the following spring, in a shallow nest at ground level. She may guard the nest for a few nights, then return to her burrow underground. The eggs incubate for about a year, so hatchlings emerge about the time that eggs are being laid the following season. Evidence indicates the gender of tuatara hatchlings is determined by both genetic and environmental factors. It is said that it is more likely for warmer eggs to produce male tuatara, and cooler eggs to produce females. The hatchlings receive no parental care and need to find their own food.

Tuatara live for a relatively long time, reaching reproductive maturity at about 15 years, and may breed for many decades. Their maximum lifespan is not known for certain, but many tuatara have reached 80 years still looking vigorous and healthy. Tuatara live in underground burrows and are more active at night, but will come out during the day to bask in the sun. Both sexes are territorial, and males aggressively defend their territory by posing and fighting if necessary. Teeth are their main weapons, and a bite can cause serious injury. Tuatara are carnivorous, eating invertebrates, lizards and the baby seabirds with which they often share burrows.

Tuatara were once widespread and abundant on the New Zealand mainland, but when Polynesian settlers arrived in New Zealand, in about 1250-1300 AD, they brought with them Pacific rats which killed tuatara. By the time of European settlement, in the 1840s, tuatara were almost extinct on the New Zealand mainland. Some islands provided temporary havens, but soon these too began to be invaded by rats and other mammalian predators.

Gradually tuatara became restricted to 32 nearshore islands. Many of these islands were tiny, some as small as only one hectare. A few, such as the Poor Knights common tuatara lives on islands off the north-eastern coast of New Zealand, and on some islands in Cook Strait. The Brothers Island tuatara survived only on the of the Brothers Island tuatara have been created on Titi Island in the Marlborough Sounds, and on Somes Island in Wellington Harbour.

Tuatara can live in remarkably dense populations. Most tuatara islands have 50-100 tuatara per square hectare - so an island of only 10 hectares may have a population of hundreds. Larger islands with many seabirds and invertebrates, which tuatara eat, may have greater densities. The largest population is on Stephens Island, where there are estimated to be as many as 2,500 per hectare in some places, and a total of at least 30,000. The total number of tuatara on all the islands is estimated to be between 50,000 and 100,000.

Legal protection, was granted to tuatara and the islands they occupied in 1895, but the reptiles continued to decline. Since then, active conservation management has reversed the decline, and new populations have become established on predator-free islands. In the mid-1980s the New Zealand Wildlife Service and its successor, the Department of Conservation, developed ways to eradicate rats from islands. Rats have now gone from almost all of the tuatara islands, making them safe for many threatened native species. In addition, the collection by conservationists of eggs for incubation in captivity, breeding in captivity, and moving tuatara to rat islands off the Northland coast, or Stephens Island in Cook Strait, were never invaded by rats, and had few of the other mammals that threaten native animals. The tiny, 4 hectare North Brother Island, in Cook Strait. However, two new populations free islands, have increased the number of islands that are inhabited by tuatara to 37. Many new tuatara populations are planned for islands and mainland reserves that have been freed of predators.

The Tasmanian tiger, or thylacine, was a carnivorous marsupial (a meat-eating mammal which carries its young in a pouch). It was given the name ‘tiger’ because it had striped fur, and because it was ferocious. Between 24 million and 15 million years ago, many types of thylacine roamed across Australia, their powerful jaws playing a role in maintaining a balance in the ecosystems of their day. Some species were for sized, while others were barely the size of kittens.

But when a period of climate change cooled Australia about 12 million years ago, the numbers of these ancient thylacines began to decline. By about 3 million years ago, only one species was left. About 4,000 years ago, these vanished completely from the Australian mainland, so that Tasmania, a large island to the south of Australia, became the last remaining place where thylacines existed. They ruled the island's animal life unchallenged until Europeans - with sheep, dogs and a great indifference to native flora and fauna - seem to have brought about their extinction. In 1936, the last captive Tasmanian tiger died in Hobart Zoo. Since then, many expeditions have searched for tigers in the Tasmanian bush, but no definitive evidence has been found. Despite this, there are many who keep searching.

In 1981 Dutch - born zoologist Hans Naarding was in Tasmania conducting a survey of Latham’s snipe, a species of endangered bird. One night he saw an animal in the light from the searchlight mounted on his vehicle. He described as about the size of a large dog, but with slightly sloping hindquarters and a fairly thick tail continuing straight on from its backbone. He said that it had 12 distinct stripes on its back, running down to the point where the tail began. He reported the sighting to the Director of Tasmania’s National Parks. ‘When the news broke,’ said Naarding, ‘I was besieged by television crews, including four or five from Japan, and others from the United Kingdom, Germany, New Zealand and South America.’ Government and private search parties combed the region, but no further sightings were made. The tiger, as always, had escaped to its lair - a place that many insist exists only in the imagination. Others disagree. There have been more than 4,000 claimed sightings of the animal since supposedly died out, and the average number of claims reported to the authorities each year is now 150. So is it out there? Even experts differ in opinion.

Randolph Rose, Associate Professor of Zoology at the University of Tasmania, says that he dreamed of seeing a thylacine, but is now convinced that his dream will go unfulfilled. The consensus among conservationists is that any animal with from the Australian mainland, so that Tasmania, a large island to the south of a population base of less than 1,000 headed for extinction within 60 years. Sixty years ago, he says, ‘there was only one thylacine that we know of, and that was in Hobart Zoo. Take it from me, the tiger is gone.’ But Dr David Pemberton, curator of zoology at the Tasmanian Museum states that, despite scientific thinking that a relatively large number of animals required to sustain a population the Florida panther is down to a dozen or so animals, and, while it does have some inbreeding problems, is still ticking along. After all, animals can be notoriously elusive. The strange fish known as coelacanth, with its ’proto legs‘, was thought to have died out with the dinosaurs 700 million years ago until a specimen was dragged to the surface in a shark net off the coast of South Africa in 1938.

Wildlife biologist Nick Mooney has the unenviable task of investigating all so-called sightings of the tiger. It was Mooney who was first consulted in late February 2005 about the authenticity of new digital photographic images of a thylacine allegedly taken by a tourist. On the face value, Mooney says, this particular account of a sighting and the photographs submitted as proof amount to one of the most convincing cases for the species survival that he has seen. Many other sightings have been hoaxes, and many sincere seekers are victims of obsession. ‘It is a blind optimism that something is, rather than a something isn’t.’ Mooney says. ‘If something crosses the road, it’s not a case of ‘I wonder what that was?’. Rather, it is a case of ‘That’s a thylacine!’

However, Mooney treats sightings on face value. ‘I never try to embarrass people,’ he says, ‘but the fact that I don’t pack the car immediately after they telephone can be taken as ridicule. Obsessive characters get angry that someone in my position is not out there when they think the thylacine is there.’

Hans Naarding, whose sighting of a striped animal two decades ago was the highlight of a lifetime of animal spotting, remains puzzled by the time and money people waste on tiger searches. He says resources would be better applied to saying another endangered animal, the Tasmanian devil, and helping declining migratory bird populations. Could the thylacine still be out there? ‘Sure,’ Naarding says, ‘I know the vast south - west wilderness of Tasmania well. They could survive … .’

But, if this is the case, it will not be long before they do disappear completely. Naarding believes that any discovery of surviving thylacines would be rather pointless. How do you bring a species back from extinction? He asks ‘What could you do with it? If there are thylacines out there, they are better off right where they are.’

Spray-painted graffiti can be seen on city walls or on trains in many cities, and New York is no exception. Since the late eighties, New York City’s policy on graffiti has been based on the broken windows thesis. This theory, introduced in 1982 In Atlantic Monthly by James Q Wilson and George L Kelling, argues that petty non-violent crimes such as the creation of graffiti increase overall crime. The theory reasons that if minor signs of disorder such as broken windows and graffiti are left unfixed, potential criminals assume that chaos reigns, and commit more crimes. As Lieutenant Steve Mona of the New York City Vandal Squad state in his anti-graffiti program, ‘Graffiti gives the look of disorder, as if nobody is in control. Graffiti is the first sign that a neighborhood is falling apart.’

New York has spent a large amount of time and money fighting graffiti in the belief that these efforts will send a message that there is someone in charge, and overall crime will fall. However, while the application of the ‘broken windows' thesis is credited by some as causing the fall in crime in New York, there is little evidence supporting this. Instead, many criminologists attribute the reduction in crime to a collection of causes, only one of which is the attention to small, visible crime by the police. However, of these small crimes, graffiti still gets a particularly bad rap from the New York City Transit Authority. According to its website, 'Graffiti has long been viewed as the most obvious sign of urban blight.' Reasons for concern expressed by the Mayor of New York about the presence of graffiti include the belief that graffiti is a threat to the quality of life in the city, and that it leads to greater acts of crime. The Mayor also argues that it causes millions of dollars of damage to property holders and to the city, and that graffiti tags (decorated initials) are a means of communication for gangs.

While the Mayor's contentions are valid, they only apply to the most degenerate types of graffiti. City administrators lump together all forms of graffiti: artistic, meaningful, and gang-or drug-related, into one undesirable group. This oversimplifies the realities of street art. Graffiti artist Dmitri Wright comments: 'Graft has a multitude of forms and meanings but a lot of the connotations of the art form and how it is linked to street culture create a divide. All its opponents need to do is look at some of it. It is absolutely spectacular, but sometimes people can't get past their own culture.'

The beautiful graffiti-art that can be found today throughout the city, on commissioned walls and in art galleries, is an expression of New York like no other art form. Its artists either come from the city itself or are drawn to the city from around the world. Surely, in the right context, graffiti-art can become a powerful tool to promote New York City’s identity and originality. Although graffiti first emerged as an illegal form of expression, its influence on the art world is increasingly present, and many large-scale pieces are impressive not only in their size, but also in their artistic themes and techniques. Today, New York graffiti-art on canvas can sell for tens of thousands of dollars.

Graffiti New York-style has its roots in a social movement of young people in the seventies and eighties, and the themes in graffiti-art were undeniably a reflection of social factors at play in New York. The city's youths wanted to speak out about the issues that affected them and have their messages heard Kids with nothing more than ingenuity could gain recognition as minor celebrities. Graffiti artist King Bee explains: 'In the world of graffiti, every writer or artist, one way or another, participates in the fame game. They all seek recognition for their creativity in the who's who in the graffiti game.'

Graffiti grew in part out of a reaction to the fact that the city was becoming covered in advertisements. City administrators did not see the connection between the rise of advertising saturating the landscape, and the increasing saturation of the city with graffiti. It was a natural progression that the youth of the day would use the same tools to sell themselves that the corporations were using to sell products to the public.

When considering approaches to the graffiti issue, there should be more productive ways to combat graffiti than simply banning it. The most common alternative suggested is creating a legitimate outlet for the graffiti urges of young people, Private groups such as The Phun Phactony have put this concept into action. Pat DiLillo, founder of The Phun Phactory, explains the logic behind his organization: 'I figured if I created a place for the young people to paint [graffiti], then it would eliminate the legal graffiti. Many of these artists start out as vandals. There is nothing for them to do; there's no youth program or anything.’

Many graffiti pieces in the city, far from being related to juvenile delinquency, are dedicated to powerful social issues. Though their messages may be the same, ties between the city and graft artists are rarely sought and never formed, although many socially influenced pieces display the potential for creating such bonds, By providing a legal medium for the artistic impulses of the city’s youth, the city could form a relationship with that generation as well as gain a beautified urban environment.

segments.text: Part one, you will hear a man phoning Community Learning Center to get information about the sports photography course it offers.

segments.text: Good morning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Community Learning Center.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What can I do for you?

segments.text: Oh, hello.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm calling about the sports photography course you offer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I learned about it from an advert somewhere in the newspaper.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: May I have your name, please?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thank you, Mr.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Johnson.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is there anything in particular you would like to know?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'm eager to improve my photography skills.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: You know, my son has just joined the school football team this semester, and I want to keep a visual record of all these precious moments.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But when I took shots, they were often too blurry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: You see, I'm no expert, so I'd like to find out about the level of the course to see if it's suitable for me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Well, this course is intended for beginners only.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But there will be an advance course for experienced photographers next semester.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's good to know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I think this course works for me just fine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Do I have to go for an interview to register?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There's no need to do that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have plenty of vacancies right now, so if you plan to register, I can sign you up over the phone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But before that, how much does it cost?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It was $45 last year for a single student.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Luckily, this year we have more funding, so the price has gone down to $38.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Oh, good.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So when will the next course start?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let me check.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Just a minute.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's Monday today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So there was a course that ended just last weekend.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Then there's another one starting from April the 17th.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But if you miss this one, the next one is from May the first.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's too late.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'll just register for the next course then.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: May I take your phone number?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, I've made a note of that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: When you come to take the first lesson, please bring two photos that you've taken.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Is there any special requirements for the photos?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You reminded me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The weather of the two shots should be different.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Like one on a sunny day and another on a snowy day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yes, exactly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now listen and answer questions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So apart from the photos, do I need to prepare anything else for the course?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Nothing more.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Do you have a syllabus for the course?

segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You can download it from our website.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Just Keen Community Learning Center of Pinewood.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You can also come over to the center and get a copy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'll just download it online, but can you please introduce the course in detail?

segments.text: The course covers two days, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On Saturday morning, the instructor will explain all the basics of amateur and professional sports photography and the differences between them, followed by instructions on the use of specific equipment for various sports, like long lenses and mono pots for shooting football matches.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's exactly what I need to know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What about the rest of the course.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On Saturday afternoon?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is normally a workshop on the technical side of things for the photos that your classmates have brought.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You'll have to work together to decide the best position to take the shots.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Oh, that's interesting.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On Sunday, there's a workshop taking place in a computer equipped room where you'll learn to edit different shots.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That sounds challenging.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Indeed it is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is also a section on some tricks to sell them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2

segments.speaker: Speaker 1

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd love to.
